name: Colin Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the orchards at Ferris Bros, sixty hectares of apples and pears, plus a few fields of grass we cut for hay. In winter it's pruning, row after row, and in spring it's frost nights and spraying for scab. At picking time I run a crew of thirty and the cold store. I use an AI app now and then for pest forecasts and frost alerts, but I still go out with a torch at three in the morning to check the thermometer myself.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pruning, honestly. It's slow and quiet, and you're shaping a tree for the next twenty years. Old Mr Ferris taught me when I was sixteen, as an apprentice, and I'll do the same for some kid one day. The pay's low for what I do, I've got maybe two weeks' money saved, and Grace and I rent a little house near the packhouse where she works in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Suits me fine. The frost app gets a bit better, and life goes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was a handy tool, not a revolution. It helps me with forecasts and paperwork, but trees still need someone who knows them. I'd say it at the growers' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. My real worries are frost, cheap imports and whether Ferris Bros keeps paying for my hours. Nothing about this picture changes those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am and keep using the AI app for frost and pest warnings, maybe a bit more for the spray records. I'd talk to Mr Ferris about taking on an apprentice next year. And I'd try to save a bit more, maybe by growing our own veg.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a still spring night with no frost forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprentice, when money's tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how I learned, and it's how the orchard survives. Trees outlive the people who plant them. If nobody learns pruning, it doesn't matter how good the app is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Cheap imports, you said. Who do you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. It's a market, and shoppers want cheap apples. Our job is to grow better ones, and to tell people why they're worth paying for.

S0.say: I'd say AI was a handy tool, not a revolution, helping with forecasts and paperwork. Trees still need someone who knows them.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because my real worries are frost, cheap imports and whether the business keeps paying for my hours. Nothing in this picture changes those.
S0.do: Carries on and uses the AI app a little more for frost, pest and spray records. Asks the owner to take on an apprentice and tries to save more by growing his own vegetables.
S0.feel: Calm, like a still spring night with no frost forecast.
S0.quote: Trees outlive the people who plant them.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is calm, patient and anchored in apprenticeship: he was taught at sixteen and wants to pass it on. He uses AI tools selectively and still checks the thermometer himself. His free-market view shows when he blames nobody for cheap imports. Long time horizons, trees over twenty years, run through how he talks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds more like what's actually happening. There's already a robot picker being tested in a big orchard south of here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and good growers will adapt. Robots might pick, but someone still needs to understand the trees. I'd say young people should still learn the trade properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think picking crews shrink first and my job changes. I'd be managing robots and fewer people. That's okay if Ferris Bros keeps me on and trains me, but I'd miss the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for a couple of orchards to prove the robot pickers work, then ask to trial one on our pears. I'd learn the software when the time came, through the supplier. Meanwhile I'd keep pruning and push to keep an apprentice on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. I'd want proof before I got excited or scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stefan, who's been picking with us for nine years. He's the best picker we've got, gentle with the fruit. If a robot picks, he's the first to lose out, and that's not fair on him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pears first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're easier for a robot to see and they hang more evenly on our trees. And if it bruises a few, it's not the end of the world. I'd never start on the Cox apples.

S1.say: I'd say change is coming and good growers will adapt, but someone still needs to understand the trees. Young people should still learn the trade properly.
S1.think: I think picking crews shrink first and my job turns into managing robots and fewer people. That's fine if I'm kept on and trained, though I'd miss the crew.
S1.do: Waits for other orchards to prove robot pickers, then asks to trial one on the pears. Learns the supplier's software when needed and pushes to keep an apprentice on.
S1.feel: Uneasy but okay, wanting proof before feeling excited or scared.
S1.quote: I'd never start on the Cox apples.
S1.fieldNote: Colin follows a steady rule: let others prove it, then trial carefully on the least risky crop. He named a long-serving picker and felt it was unfair on him. Apprenticeship keeps coming back as his main value. He expects to keep a changed job and is fairly calm about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two picking seasons. Good grief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and that people need real work, not just payments. Businesses will do what they have to, but communities need to hold together. I'd say it at the growers' meeting and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Ferris Bros would sell to a big company or automate everything. A robot that can prune, pick and manage the cold store doesn't need me. I'd have two weeks' savings and a rent bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, Grace and I would cut back to the bone and stop saving for our holiday. I'd ask Mr Ferris if there's any job left, maybe looking after the machines. If not, I'd look for work in town or on a building site, and Grace and I might move in with my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like a tree cut at the base.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, there's nothing to plan. I couldn't learn a new trade, couldn't save, couldn't see where things were going. With longer I'd move with it, like with the slower one. Two years just knocks you down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the apprentice you wanted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part that'd really get me. There'd be no point taking one on. Whatever I know about pruning would just stop with me.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and people need real work, not just payments. Businesses will do what they must, but communities need to hold together.
S2.think: I think the business would sell or automate fully, and a robot that prunes, picks and runs the cold store doesn't need me. I'd have two weeks' savings and a rent bill.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the bone and drops holiday savings at once. Asks the owner about looking after the machines, and otherwise seeks work in town or on building sites, possibly moving in with his parents.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like a tree cut at the base.
S2.quote: Whatever I know about pruning would just stop with me.
S2.fieldNote: The loss Colin felt most was not his wage but the end of passing on pruning skills. He doesn't blame his employer, consistent with his free-market views. His plan is defensive and family-based. The tree image came naturally to him and was striking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a few seasons to see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to adapt if we're sensible. Growers should learn the new machines and train young people for what's still needed. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose the orchard manager job in three or four years. But I could learn to manage the robots and save a bit, and maybe set up something of my own. I don't know what yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start saving fifty pounds a month and cancel the car loan by selling the newer car. When robot pickers were proven, I'd get trained on them and ask to lead the changeover. By year two I'd look at grafting and supplying young trees, because people will still plant orchards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. Like a frosty night where you've got the fans ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Grafting young trees. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's skilled, it's slow, and it's still about trees. Even if robots run the orchards, someone has to grow the trees they pick from. And I learned it from Mr Ferris, so I'd be using what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, especially in the grafting. A small nursery with one apprentice, that's my kind of business. I'd want to pass it on before the machines take everything.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to adapt if we're sensible. Growers should learn the new machines and train young people for what's still needed.
S3.think: I think I'd lose the manager job in three or four years, but I could learn the robots, save and maybe start something of my own. I don't know what yet.
S3.do: Saves fifty pounds a month and sells the newer car to clear the loan. Trains on proven robot pickers and leads the changeover, then looks at grafting and supplying young trees by year two.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, like a frosty night with the fans ready.
S3.quote: Even if robots run the orchards, someone has to grow the trees they pick from.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Colin builds a sensible plan: lead the changeover, then move into a small tree nursery. The idea uses skills his mentor taught him and lets him keep an apprentice. He still waits for proof before acting. Selling the car was a real, concrete cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to plant an orchard and see it fruit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to prepare properly, and young people should still learn the trade. Growers should adapt bit by bit. There's no need to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine if I used the time well. I'd learn the machines, save, and slowly build up the grafting business. The risk is that I'd get comfortable and leave it too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep my job, save a little and start grafting a few hundred trees in a corner of Mr Ferris's land. I'd get trained on the robots once they'd been running elsewhere for a season. By year four or five I'd aim to be running the nursery properly with one apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything else for you and Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably get married sooner rather than later, and think about kids. With ten years I'd feel there was some ground under us. With two, we'd put all that off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might get comfortable. How would you stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace would stop me. She's sharper than me with dates and plans. She'd put the grafting days on the calendar and make sure I turned up.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time to prepare properly, and young people should still learn the trade. Growers should adapt bit by bit without panic.
S4.think: I think I'd be fine if I used the time well, learning the machines and slowly building a grafting business. The risk is getting comfortable and leaving it too late.
S4.do: Keeps his job, saves a little and starts grafting a few hundred trees on spare land in year one. Trains on robots once proven elsewhere and aims to run a nursery with an apprentice by year four or five.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd feel there was some ground under us.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years gives Colin both a business plan and the confidence to marry and think about children. He knows he might drift and relies on his partner's planning. His values stay steady across scenarios: apprenticeship, patience and trees. He is calmest of all here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd lose the job and there'd be no point training anyone, so the skills would just end with me. What would help is help for small businesses like a tree nursery to get started, and apprenticeships kept going for trades people will still need.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the trees themselves. They live fifty years. Whatever happens with AI, someone should be thinking about the orchards our grandchildren will pick from.

headlineQuote: Even if robots run the orchards, someone has to grow the trees they pick from.
portrait: Colin Fischer is 27 and manages sixty hectares of apples and pears, having learned the trade as a sixteen-year-old apprentice. He rents a small house with his partner Grace, who works in the packhouse office, and has about two weeks of savings. He uses AI apps now and then for frost and pest alerts but always checks the trees himself, and he waits for proof before adopting new kit. In the slower scenarios he plans to lead the change to robot pickers and then start a small tree nursery with an apprentice; in the two-year picture what hurts most is that his pruning skills would end with him. Longer warning gives him the confidence to marry and think about children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd lose his job and there would be no point training an apprentice, so his skills would end with him.
whatWouldHelp: Help for small businesses like a tree nursery to start, and apprenticeships kept going for trades that are still needed.
